newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Plan for duties on Norwegian salmon opposed.
newsitem.headline: Plan for duties on Norwegian salmon opposed.

text.p: Some European Union countries oppoose or have doubts about a European Commission proposal to slap anti-dumping duties on imports of farmed Norwegian salmon, EU sources said on Tuesday.

The EU executive is considering an average duty of 13.7 percent on Norwegian salmon imports, accusing the country's producers of receiving state subsidies and dumping the fish on the EU market at less than the cost of production.
The EU's anti-dumping committee -- which consists of officials from the 15 member states -- discussed the sensitive issue at a closed meeting in Brussels on Monday.
There was a surprising amount of criticism of the proposal and the Commission's arguments failed to convince those member states with doubts, one EU source said. "There was no enthusiasm," he added.
But a Commission source disputed this view of the meeting, saying he believed a majority of member states were in favour of Trade Commissioner Sir Leon Brittan's proposal.

More importantly, the EU executive has the power to impose provisional duties for a period of six months without the consent of member states and it was unclear whether it would take on board any member states' doubts.
The EU source said only Britain and Ireland -- which also farm salmon -- fully and openly supported Brittan's recommendation to impose the duties, the source said.

Denmark, Germany, the Netherlands and Sweden were said to oppose or to be sceptical about the arguments in favour of introducing such import duties. Most countries had not yet taken a definite position, asking instead for more information.
"Many countries are advocating a negotiated solution," the source said.

"If there appears to be a large majority against I think the Commission will try to find a negotiated settlement with the Norwegians," said another EU source. He stressed, however, that the views of several member states were not yet clear.

The European Commission launched the inquiry in September, looking into Scottish complaints that imports of salmon from Norway were being subsidised and dumped, depressing prices and hurting the EU industry.

Norway, which is a member of the 18-nation European Economic Area but whose voters rejected EU membership in 1994, is lobbying heavily to avert the threat of punitive duties on exports worth seven billion Norwegian crowns ($1.0 billion).
On Monday, Norwegian Foreign Minister Bjoern Tore Godal called for further talks with the EU to settle the row.
"It's an issue which should be solved between good neighbours, not hostile third parties," Godal said after talks with EU External Affairs Commissioner Hans van den Broek.
Godal is due to discuss the issue with Brittan on Wednesday. -- Brussels newsroom +32 2 287 68 11
